text: With the build validated last lesson, it's time to actually submit jobs to real hardware. This lesson is about doing that in a way that produces a trustworthy, analyzable record — not just a folder of disconnected numbers.

This lesson covers what metadata every real-hardware run needs recorded, how to apply earlier controls like interleaving when you're the one submitting jobs, a practical run log format you can reuse for any capstone, and how to handle the realities of shared cloud hardware queues without compromising your design.

Every job should have recorded, at the moment it runs: the exact device name, the calibration timestamp, the exact transpiled circuit and shot count, and a timestamp for submission versus actual execution — queue time itself is diagnostically useful data, not just overhead. Reconstructing this after the fact is unreliable, since devices recalibrate and you can't answer later which device state a run actually used if you didn't capture it at the time.

In practice, applying earlier lessons' interleaving means submitting your two conditions close together in real time, even though the queue system ultimately decides execution order. In a worked run log entry, a three-qubit job and a five-qubit job, both at scaling factor one, are submitted within a minute of each other and both execute against the same calibration window, roughly forty-five minutes apart — exactly the interleaving earlier lessons called for, made concrete and auditable in a plain spreadsheet or JSON-lines file.

Real queue behavior to expect: wait time varies by time of day and platform demand, providers may prioritize differently for paid versus free tiers, and a device can go offline for maintenance mid-project, possibly forcing a hardware switch. None of this is a flaw in your design — it's the actual operating environment applied quantum computing research runs in, and documenting it honestly, rather than pretending your conditions were cleaner than they were, is itself good research practice.

Next lesson is where the data actually answers your research question — mapping what you collected back onto the specific claims in your original hypothesis, not a vague impression of whether it worked.
